passages.t: War with the Philistines, and an army in hiding
passages.happening:
The chapter opens with the usual notice of a king's age and the length of his reign (verse 1). Saul chooses three thousand men. Two thousand stay with him at Michmash and in the hill country of Bethel, and a thousand go with his son Jonathan at Gibeah (verse 2).

Jonathan attacks the Philistine outpost at Geba, and the Philistines hear of it. Saul blows the ram's horn through the land, and Israel hears that it has become ‘a stench to the Philistines’ (verse 4). The people are called to join Saul at Gilgal.

The Philistines gather with three thousand chariots, six thousand horsemen, ‘and troops as numerous as the sand on the seashore’, and camp at Michmash (verse 5). Israel's men see the danger and hide ‘in caves and thickets, among the rocks, and in cellars and cisterns’ (verse 6). Some even cross the Jordan into Gad and Gilead. Saul stays at Gilgal, ‘and all his troops were quaking in fear’ (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
Verse 1 has a well-known problem in the text. Read word for word, the Hebrew says that Saul was one year old when he became king and reigned two years over Israel. It seems to keep the usual formula with the numbers damaged or missing. English Bibles fill the gaps in different ways. The Berean Standard Bible gives thirty and forty-two, and Paul's sermon in Acts speaks of forty years. In verse 5 the Hebrew reads thirty thousand chariots, and the BSB follows Greek and Syriac copies with three thousand. Neither problem changes the story, but a careful reader should know these figures are reconstructed.

The Philistines had settled on the southern coast in the twelfth century BC and were pushing into the hill country. Michmash, Geba and Gibeah lay a few miles north of the later Jerusalem, in Benjamin, Saul's own tribe. Michmash and Geba faced each other across a steep ravine. So the Philistine camp at Michmash sat in the heart of Saul's homeland.

The narrator builds the pressure step by step: an army like the sand, soldiers hiding in caves and cisterns, some fleeing across the Jordan, and the rest shaking with fear.
passages.later:
Israel had hidden in the same way in the days of the judges, when ‘the Israelites prepared shelters for themselves in the mountains, caves, and strongholds’ (Judges 6:2).

Paul's sermon in Acts gives the length of Saul's reign as a round number: ‘God gave them forty years under Saul son of Kish’ (Acts 13:21).
passages.asks: Israel's soldiers hid in caves and cisterns when they saw the size of the enemy. Ask what you hide from when the trouble in front of you looks too big. And ask what it would mean to stand where you were told to stand, as Saul did for a while at Gilgal.

passages.happening:
“And Saul waited seven days for the time appointed by Samuel, but Samuel did not come to Gilgal, and the troops began to desert Saul” (verse 8).

So he said, “Bring me the burnt offering and the peace offerings.” ‘And he offered up the burnt offering’ (verse 9). Just as he finishes, Samuel arrives (verse 10).

“What have you done?” Samuel asked (verse 11). Saul explains: the troops were leaving, Samuel had not come at the set time, and the Philistines were gathering. He feared they would attack before he had sought the LORD's favor. ‘So I felt compelled to offer the burnt offering’ (verse 12).

“You have acted foolishly,” Samuel declared. “You have not kept the command that the LORD your God gave you; if you had, the LORD would have established your kingdom over Israel for all time” (verse 13). “But now your kingdom will not endure; the LORD has sought a man after His own heart and appointed him ruler over His people, because you have not kept the command of the LORD” (verse 14).

Samuel leaves, and Saul counts the men still with him: about six hundred (verse 15).
passages.hearers:
In chapter 10 Samuel had told Saul to wait seven days at Gilgal until he came to offer the sacrifices and tell him what to do (10:8). Before a battle, Israel's armies sought the LORD's favor with a sacrifice.

The problem was not simply that a king offered a sacrifice. Kings elsewhere in that world often acted as chief priests, and later David and Solomon are said to offer sacrifices. The problem was that Saul disobeyed the prophet's plain word. He treated God's favor as something the ritual could secure without the LORD's messenger.

The narrator lets the pressure build and then gives one sentence of action, and at once Samuel is there. Samuel's question, ‘What have you done?’, recalls God's question to the woman in the garden. Saul's answer is a string of reasons. He blames the troops, then Samuel, then the Philistines, and only then says that he felt compelled.

Samuel calls it foolish. In the Old Testament, foolishness is less about a lack of intelligence than about living as though God's word did not matter. Saul acted from what looked like good sense. Samuel calls it folly.

A man after his own heart has been read in two ways: a man whose heart matches God's, or a man of God's own choosing. Both readings have defenders, and both fit David's story. Saul's kingdom, his line on the throne, will not endure. The verdict falls on his dynasty, and he goes on reigning for years.
passages.later:
Samuel's question echoes God's question in the garden: “What is this you have done?” (Genesis 3:13).

Paul, preaching in Acts, quotes Samuel's words about the man after God's heart: ‘I have found David son of Jesse a man after My own heart; he will carry out My will in its entirety’ (Acts 13:22). He joins them with a psalm: ‘I have found My servant David; with My sacred oil I have anointed him’ (Psalm 89:20).
passages.hard:
Why was Saul punished so severely for offering a sacrifice a little early, when he was trying to seek God's favor?

Many readers feel the sentence is out of proportion to the offense. Several answers are given. Some stress that Saul broke a specific command given through the prophet by whom the LORD guided Israel's king (10:8). The question was whether the king would rule under God's word or over it. Others point to his reply. He blames everyone else and shows no sorrow, a pattern chapter 15 will confirm. Some also note that the judgment falls on Saul's dynasty, that his kingdom will not last, and not at once on his throne, since he reigns for years after.

Readers still differ on how to weigh these. What the text insists on is that the first king must learn that his authority comes from God, and that no religious act can take the place of obedience, as Samuel will say plainly in chapter 15.
passages.asks: Saul waited almost long enough, and then felt compelled to act. Ask where you are tempted to fix things yourself because God seems late. And ask whether your explanations for disobedience, like Saul's, put the blame on everyone else first.

passages.happening:
Saul and Jonathan and their men are at Geba of Benjamin, and the Philistines are camped at Michmash (verse 16). Raiders go out from the Philistine camp in three companies, toward Ophrah, toward Beth-horon, and toward the border overlooking the Valley of Zeboim (verses 17-18).

No blacksmith can be found in all Israel, because the Philistines have said, “The Hebrews must not be allowed to make swords or spears” (verse 19). Israel has to go down to the Philistines even to sharpen its farm tools (verse 20). ‘The charge was a pim for sharpening a plowshare or mattock’ (verse 21).

So on the day of battle no one with Saul and Jonathan has a sword or spear. ‘Only Saul and his son Jonathan had weapons’ (verse 22).
passages.hearers:
The Philistines controlled the making and mending of metal tools and weapons. Israel depended on its enemies even to sharpen a plow. Whether this was a monopoly on iron working or simply on smiths and forges is debated, but the effect is clear.

The word pim was unknown to earlier translators. The King James Version guessed that it meant a file. Then small stone weights inscribed with the word turned up in excavations in Israel. They weigh about two thirds of a shekel. The verse turned out to be a price list. A shekel then was a weight of silver, not a coin.

The chapter ends with an inventory of Israel's weakness: six hundred men, raiders loose in the land, and only two swords. Saul has a crown and almost nothing else. The next chapter will show what God can do with a few.
passages.later: The Song of Deborah describes Israel just as poorly armed in an earlier generation: ‘Not a shield or spear was found among forty thousand in Israel’ (Judges 5:8).
passages.asks: Israel had only two swords. Ask what you think you need before you can obey God, and whether that is really true. And ask what it means that the next chapter's victory begins with exactly this weakness.
